learn.hook: Ask five people what 'a better life' means and you may get five different answers — and some of them may even clash!
points: Development means progress, but people do not all want the same things. Each person's development goals depend on their life situation.
A landless rural labourer may want more days of work and better wages; a prosperous farmer may want higher prices for crops; a girl in a city may want the same freedom as her brother.
Goals can conflict: a big dam may give electricity to industries and cities, but it may submerge villages and force families to move. Development for one group can mean loss for another.
People want more income, but they also seek non-material things: equal treatment, freedom, security, respect from others and friendship.

Some things money cannot buy for one person alone: a pollution-free environment, medicines that are not adulterated, or protection from infectious diseases. These usually need the whole community or the government to act together.

example.q: Think it through: Arjun gets two job offers. Job A pays ₹5,000 more per month but is in a faraway city with no job security. Job B pays a little less, is close to his family and is permanent. What should he consider?
steps: Income matters: Job A gives more money each month.
Non-income factors also matter: job security, time with family, a safe working atmosphere and chances to learn.
Job B offers security and family support, which money alone cannot buy.
So the choice depends on Arjun's own goals — there is no single answer that is right for everyone.
example.answer: Both income and non-income goals matter; the 'better' job depends on what Arjun values most.

learn.reallife: When your family discusses moving to a new city for a job, they think about salary, but also schools, safety, distance from grandparents and the neighbourhood — that is development thinking in action.

games.title: Who wants what?
pairs: More days of work and better wages
Girl from a well-off urban family
As much freedom as her brother
Villager living where a dam is planned

games.title: Development goals: true or false?
items: Different people can have different development goals.
Goals depend on each person's life situation, so they differ.
What is development for one person can be harmful for another.
A dam can power factories but displace the villagers whose land goes under water.
People care only about earning more money.
People also want freedom, equality, security and respect.
A clean environment is something one family can easily buy for itself.
Clean air and water need collective action by the community or government.
Job security can matter as much as salary when choosing a job.
Many people value a secure, permanent job along with income.
Equal treatment and respect are examples of non-material goals.
They cannot be measured in rupees but are important for a good life.

quiz.q: Which development goal would a landless rural labourer most likely have?
options: Higher support prices for the crops he grows
More days of work and better wages
quiz.explain: A landless labourer does not own land or a factory; he depends on wages, so more work and better pay are his main goals.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the goals of a labourer with those of a landowning farmer or industrialist

quiz.q: A dam will give electricity to cities but will submerge several villages. What does this show about development?
options: Development goals can conflict: one group's gain may be another's loss
Dams are always bad for everyone
Development goals are the same for all people
quiz.explain: City users and industries gain power, while villagers lose their homes and land, so their goals clash.
quiz.mistake: Assumes everyone gains equally from a development project

quiz.q: Which of these is a non-material development goal?
options: Being treated with respect and equality
quiz.explain: Respect and equal treatment cannot be bought or measured in money, so they are non-material goals.
quiz.mistake: Thinks only things that can be bought count as goals

quiz.q: Which of these is hardest for one family to buy with its own money?
quiz.explain: Clean air and water depend on what everyone around does, so they need community or government action, not one family's spending.
quiz.mistake: Believes money alone can buy every good thing in life

quiz.q: Dengue spreads through mosquitoes breeding in stagnant water. What is the most effective protection for a colony?
options: Each family buying an expensive gadget for itself
Everyone together clearing stagnant water across the whole colony
Ignoring it, since only some houses are affected
quiz.explain: Mosquitoes fly from house to house, so protection works only when the whole community acts together.
quiz.mistake: Thinks private spending can replace collective action

quiz.q: Priya is choosing between two jobs with equal pay. Which factor is a non-income reason to prefer one job?
options: A safe working atmosphere and job security
quiz.explain: Safety and security are not about money but still make a job better. The other options are all about income.
quiz.mistake: Counts money-related benefits as non-income factors

quiz.q: Why do different people have different notions of development?
options: Because only rich people think about development
Because development has one fixed meaning for everyone
Because people's life situations, needs and hopes are different
Because the government decides every person's goals
quiz.explain: People in different situations — farmers, workers, students, business owners — need and hope for different things.
quiz.mistake: Assumes development means the same thing for all

quiz.q: Which pair shows conflicting development goals?
options: A student wants good teachers; a parent wants a good school
A farmer wants rain; another farmer wants rain too
A patient wants a nearby hospital; a doctor wants a well-equipped hospital
An industrialist wants a new factory on farmland; farmers want to keep farming that land
quiz.explain: The same land cannot be used for both, so the industrialist's goal and the farmers' goal clash.
quiz.mistake: Confuses similar or matching goals with conflicting ones

teach.ask: Gappu flaps his wings: 'Development just means getting more money, right? Why would anyone want anything else?'
teach.praise: Wow! So development is about money AND freedom, respect and security — and my goals may even clash with someone else's. Chirp-tastic!
teach.nudge: But do all people want the same things? And is money the only thing people care about?

topics.title: Per capita income: comparing countries and states

learn.hook: A cricket team's total runs don't tell you how good each batter is — and a country's total income doesn't tell you how well-off each person is!
points: Income is the most common way to compare countries: a country with more income is usually thought to be more developed, because people can buy more of what they need.
Total income is not a fair comparison, because countries have different populations. So we use average income: total income of the country ÷ its total population.

Average income is also called per capita income ('per head'). The World Bank's World Development Report uses per capita income to classify countries; it places India among low middle income countries.
An average can hide inequality: two countries can have the same average income, but in one everyone earns about the same while in the other a few are very rich and most are poor.
So per capita income is useful but incomplete — it says nothing about how income is shared or about health and education.

example.q: Think it through: Village Sundarpur has 5 families earning ₹9,000, ₹11,000, ₹10,000, ₹9,500 and ₹10,500 a month. Village Rampur has 5 families earning ₹1,000, ₹1,000, ₹1,000, ₹1,000 and ₹46,000. Compare them.
steps: Both averages are equal, but in Rampur four families earn only ₹1,000 each.
Sundarpur's income is shared far more equally, so most people would prefer to live there.
example.answer: Same average (₹10,000), but Sundarpur is more equal — averages hide how income is distributed.

learn.reallife: If a class's average marks are 70, it could be that everyone scored about 70 — or that some scored 100 and some scored 40. You need more than the average to know the full story.

items.q: Total income ₹500, people 5. Per capita income?
Total income ₹12,000, people 4. Per capita income?
Total income ₹90,000, people 30. Per capita income?
Per capita income ₹2,000, people 10. Total income?
Total income ₹45,000, people 9. Per capita income?
Per capita income ₹1,500, people 6. Total income?

items.text: Per capita income is also called ___ income.
Per capita income = total income ÷ total ___.
The World Development Report is brought out by the ___.
According to the World Bank, India is a ___ income country.
An average can hide ___ in how income is shared.

quiz.q: How is per capita income of a country calculated?
options: Total income ÷ number of workers only
quiz.explain: Per capita means 'per head', so we divide the total income by the whole population.
quiz.mistake: Divides by workers only or uses the wrong operation

quiz.q: Five families in a village earn ₹10,000, ₹12,000, ₹8,000, ₹30,000 and ₹40,000 a month. What is the average income per family?
quiz.explain: Total = ₹1,00,000. Divided among 5 families, the average is ₹20,000.
quiz.mistake: Gives the total instead of dividing by the number of families

quiz.q: Why is total income NOT a useful way to compare two countries?
options: Because total income cannot be measured
Because rich countries hide their income
Because total income is always the same for all countries
Because countries have different populations, so total income tells little about what an average person earns
quiz.explain: A big country may have a huge total income but also a huge population, so we must look at income per person.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that population size differs between countries

quiz.q: Which report classifies countries mainly by their per capita income?
options: World Development Report of the World Bank
Annual report of the Reserve Bank of India
Report of the World Trade Organisation
quiz.explain: The World Bank's World Development Report uses per capita income. The UNDP's report uses the Human Development Index instead.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the World Bank's report with UNDP's Human Development Report

quiz.q: In the World Bank's classification, in which group does India fall?
quiz.explain: India's per capita income places it among the low middle income countries.
quiz.mistake: Assumes a large total income makes India a high-income country

quiz.q: An island has a total yearly income of ₹90,00,000 and 300 people. What is its per capita income?
quiz.mistake: Makes a place-value slip while dividing large numbers

quiz.q: Country P and Country Q have the same average income. In P, everyone earns about the same; in Q, one person is very rich and the rest are poor. Where would most people prefer to live?
options: Country P, because income is shared more equally
Country Q, because it has a very rich person
Either one, since the averages are equal
Country Q, because inequality raises everyone's income
quiz.explain: With equal averages, the country with fairer distribution gives most people a better income.
quiz.mistake: Believes equal averages mean equal living conditions

quiz.q: What is the main weakness of using only per capita income to measure development?
options: It is too difficult to calculate
It does not show how income is distributed or how healthy and educated people are
It is always higher than total income
quiz.explain: Per capita income is an average; it hides inequality and says nothing about health, education or other facilities.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the average gives the complete picture of people's lives

teach.ask: Gappu is puzzled: 'My forest has more total nuts than the next forest, so all my bird friends must be richer. Right? What is per capita income?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Divide total income by the number of people to get the average — but an average can hide that some are rich and many are poor. Got it!
teach.nudge: But what do we divide the total income by? And can an average tell us whether income is shared fairly?

learn.hook: Would you rather live where people earn a little more — or where babies survive, children study and the hospital is close by?
points: Infant Mortality Rate (IMR): the number of children who die before the age of one year for every 1000 live births in that year. Literacy rate: the proportion of literate people in the 7 years and above age group. Net attendance ratio: children aged 14 and 15 attending school as a percentage of all children of that age.

A state with lower per capita income can still do better in health and education. The textbook shows Kerala with a low infant mortality rate and high literacy because it has adequate basic health and education facilities.

Many important needs are best met by public facilities provided collectively: schools, health centres, and ration shops of the Public Distribution System. Collective provision is often cheaper and reaches more people.

The UNDP's Human Development Report compares countries by their educational levels, health status and per capita income. Its Human Development Index (HDI) uses life expectancy at birth, mean years of schooling, expected years of schooling and gross national income per capita.

Sustainability: development should continue for future generations too. Groundwater is a renewable resource refilled by rain, but it gets used up if we pump it faster than it is refilled. Crude oil is non-renewable — its stock is limited and will run out.

example.q: Think it through: State X has a higher per capita income than State Y, but State X's IMR is 30 while State Y's IMR is 6. Which state has better health conditions, and why might this happen?
steps: IMR counts infant deaths per 1000 live births, so a lower IMR is better.
State Y loses 6 babies out of every 1000, State X loses 30 — State Y is far better.
Money in people's pockets cannot by itself buy vaccination drives, clean water or nearby health centres.
State Y has probably invested in public health and education facilities.
example.answer: State Y, because it has a much lower IMR; good public health facilities matter, not just income.

learn.reallife: When an anganwadi in your area gives free check-ups and nutrition to small children, or a government school gives midday meals, that is public provision improving human development.

games.title: Match the indicator to its meaning
pairs: Deaths before age one per 1000 live births
Share of literate people aged 7 and above
Children aged 14–15 attending school, as a percentage
Average expected length of life at birth

quiz.q: What does the Infant Mortality Rate (IMR) measure?
options: Number of children born per 1000 people
Number of children who die before age one per 1000 live births in a year
Number of children who go to school
Number of children below age five in a family
quiz.explain: IMR counts deaths of babies before their first birthday out of every 1000 live births in that year.
quiz.mistake: Confuses mortality (deaths) with birth rate

quiz.q: Literacy rate measures the proportion of literate people in which age group?
quiz.explain: Literacy rate is calculated for the population aged 7 years and above.
quiz.mistake: Guesses the school-starting or adult age instead of 7 years

quiz.q: In a district, there were 4000 live births in a year and 60 of these babies died before their first birthday. What is the IMR?
quiz.explain: IMR is per 1000 live births: 60 ÷ 4000 × 1000 = 15.
quiz.mistake: Gives the raw number of deaths instead of the rate per 1000

quiz.q: Which organisation publishes the Human Development Report?
quiz.explain: The Human Development Report is published by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP).
quiz.mistake: Confuses UNDP with the World Bank, which publishes the World Development Report

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT used in calculating the Human Development Index?
quiz.explain: HDI combines health (life expectancy), education (years of schooling) and income. Cars owned are not part of it.
quiz.mistake: Thinks owning luxury goods is an HDI indicator

quiz.q: According to the textbook, why does Kerala have a low infant mortality rate?
options: Because it has the highest per capita income in India
Because few babies are born there
Because it has adequate provision of basic health and educational facilities
quiz.explain: Kerala's good basic health and education facilities, not just income, keep its IMR low.
quiz.mistake: Assumes good health always comes from higher income

quiz.q: Groundwater is a renewable resource. Why can it still run short?
options: Because it is used faster than rain can refill it
Because groundwater cannot be used for farming
quiz.explain: A renewable resource is refilled by nature, but if we pump out more than is refilled, it gets overused and falls.
quiz.mistake: Thinks renewable means a resource can never run out

quiz.q: What does 'sustainable development' mean?
options: Development that meets today's needs without harming the ability of future generations to meet theirs
Development that uses up resources as fast as possible
Development that stops all use of natural resources
quiz.explain: Sustainability means development should continue for future generations, so resources and the environment must be protected.
quiz.mistake: Thinks sustainability means either using everything now or using nothing at all

teach.ask: Gappu chirps: 'If a state has more money, it must have healthier babies, right? And why do grown-ups keep saying sustainable?'
teach.praise: Hooray! So development also means health, education and public facilities — measured by HDI — and it must last for the future too!
teach.nudge: Is income enough? What about health, schooling and resources for the future?
